title: The body: breathing
hookLine: gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, breathing in long, he knows it (MN 10)

cards: You've breathed about twenty thousand times since yesterday morning. You noticed maybe three: once climbing the stairs, once in a sigh, once when something scared you. The rest happened without you.
The breath is your most faithful companion. It never takes a day off, and almost nobody pays it any attention.
The Satipatthana Sutta starts its tour of the four foundations right here: with the body, and within the body, the breath.

teach.h: THE FOREST, THE TREE, THE EMPTY HUT.
teach.b: The sutta sets the scene simply. A practitioner goes to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, legs crossed, body upright, and sets mindfulness in front of them. Then the instruction.
Breathing in long, they know, I breathe in long. Breathing out long, they know, I breathe out long. Breathing in short, they know, I breathe in short.
Breathing out short, they know that too.
Notice what isn't there: no command to breathe long, no counting, no special technique, no forcing. The breath does what it does, and the practitioner knows it. That's the first step: knowing.
They train themselves to breathe in and out experiencing the whole body. And they train themselves to breathe calming the body, letting its activity settle.

So the breath is both what you watch and what slowly quiets you. A separate sutta, the Anapanasati Sutta, expands this into sixteen steps; the tradition calls the practice anapanasati, mindfulness of in-and-out breathing.
Tradition also says it was the practice the Buddha himself used on the night of his awakening. Why start here? The breath is always available and always now.
You can't breathe yesterday's breath. Know this one, and you've arrived in the body, with the other three doors close by.

how: Mindfulness of breathing (anapanasati) is among the most widely taught Buddhist meditations; practitioners sit upright and simply know each breath as long or short, then widen to the whole body and let it calm.

o: breath control to slow the heart down on purpose
a duty to keep yourself fit and in good health
the first foundation, known first through the breath

games.q: match each step of the breathing section.
p: they know: I breathe in long

s: the sutta tells you to breathe slowly and deeply
it says to know the breath as it is, long or short; no forcing.
tradition says the Buddha used breath meditation on the night of his awakening
that's why many call it the Buddha's own practice.
a separate sutta expands breathing into sixteen steps

games.q: you sit down and notice your breath is short and shallow. what does the sutta's instruction say to do?
o: know it: breathing in short, I know I breathe in short.
games.why: the first step is only knowing. calming comes later, and it comes by itself, not by force.

practice: Sit upright, as if at the root of a tree, and let the breath come however it comes: if it's long, know it's long; if it's short, know it's short, without adjusting it.
After a few breaths, widen to the whole body breathing, belly, chest, shoulders. Then let each out-breath soften something, just a little.

wordCard.voice: The body, breathing. The first foundation begins with the breath: long, short, the whole body, calming. No forcing, only knowing.

orig.note: Pali ānāpānasati: mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing.

carryVoice: Your line: knowing the breath. Long or short, it's already happening, right now. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), mindfulness of breathing
